Coroutines are lightweight concurrency primitives that suspend without blocking the underlying thread. A `suspend` function can pause and resume; the underlying thread is free to run other coroutines while it waits.

### Vs threads
- Tens of thousands of coroutines easily co-exist on a small thread pool — threads cost megabytes of stack each.
- Suspension is cooperative; a coroutine only suspends at suspension points (`suspend fun`, `delay`, channel send/receive).
- Cancellation is cooperative (CancellationException propagates).
- **Structured concurrency** — coroutines are launched into a CoroutineScope, parent waits for children, cancellation cascades.
- Coroutines run on a CoroutineDispatcher (Default, IO, Main, Unconfined, custom).

Think of coroutines as Kotlin's answer to async/await + structured concurrency.

Structured concurrency means every coroutine has a parent that owns it, waits for it and can cancel it.

- **CoroutineScope** — defines lifetime plus context (a Job and a dispatcher). Everything launched inside becomes a child of its Job.
- **Job** — the lifecycle handle (New, Active, Completing, Cancelling, Cancelled, Completed) with parent and child links.
- **Cancellation travels both ways** — cancelling a parent cancels every child, and an uncaught child failure cancels the parent and its siblings unless the parent is a SupervisorJob.

In practice you never call `GlobalScope.launch`: it has no parent, so nothing cancels it and nothing waits for it, and the work outlives the screen that started it.

### What to use instead
- `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope` on Android, which cancel themselves at the right moment.
- `coroutineScope { }` inside a suspend function — it suspends until every child finishes and rethrows their failures.
- `supervisorScope { }` when one child's failure must not take down its siblings.
- A scope you construct with `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)` and cancel yourself in the owner's teardown.

A CoroutineDispatcher decides which thread or thread pool a coroutine runs on.

- `Dispatchers.Default` — CPU-bound work (parsing, sorting, image math). A pool sized to the CPU count.
- `Dispatchers.IO` — blocking I/O (files, JDBC, blocking sockets). An elastic pool, 64 threads by default, which shares its threads with Default so a `withContext(IO)` hop is usually cheap.
- `Dispatchers.Main` — the Android or Swing UI thread; the only place you may touch views.
- `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` — Main without a re-dispatch when you are already on it, which removes a frame of latency for UI updates.
- `Dispatchers.Unconfined` — runs in the calling thread until the first suspension; for tests and advanced cases only.
- `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n)` — a view on the IO pool capped at n threads. This is the modern way to serialize work, `n = 1` for a single SQLite writer, instead of allocating your own executor that you then have to close.

Switch with `withContext(Dispatchers.X) { ... }`, and remember that a properly written suspending library (Retrofit, Room, Ktor) already moves off the caller's thread, so wrapping its calls in `withContext(IO)` is noise.

Inject the dispatcher rather than hardcoding it, so a test can pass a `StandardTestDispatcher` from kotlinx-coroutines-test and control virtual time.

A `Flow<T>` is a cold asynchronous stream — like a `Sequence`, except its producer is allowed to suspend.

- **Cold** — nothing runs until `collect`, and every collector triggers a fresh execution of the builder.
- **Backpressure-aware** — `emit` suspends until the collector is ready, unless you insert `buffer()` or `conflate()`.
- **Cancellable** — cancelling the collecting coroutine stops the producer.
- **Operators** — `map`, `filter`, `transform`, `onEach`, `debounce`, `combine`, `flatMapLatest` / `flatMapConcat` / `flatMapMerge`, `retryWhen`, `catch`, `onCompletion`, `stateIn` / `shareIn`.

### Against the alternatives
- A `suspend fun` returns ONE value; a Flow delivers many over time.
- A `Channel` is hot and stateful: each value goes to exactly ONE consumer, and a value sent with no receiver waits in the buffer or is dropped. Use channels for work queues and hand-offs, flows for streams. `callbackFlow` is the right way to wrap a listener API, since it gives you a channel plus `awaitClose` for unregistering.

Exception transparency is the rule people get wrong: handle upstream failures with the `catch` operator, not a `try/catch` wrapped around `collect`, because operators are allowed to assume emissions never throw through them.

StateFlow always holds a current value and replays it to every new collector, while SharedFlow is a configurable broadcast hub with no value of its own.

- **StateFlow\<T>** — exactly one current value, always readable through `.value`, and conflated: a slow collector may miss intermediate updates but never the latest one. It also de-duplicates, so emitting a value equal to the current one notifies nobody.
- **SharedFlow\<T>** — configurable `replay`, `extraBufferCapacity` and `onBufferOverflow` (SUSPEND, DROP\_OLDEST, DROP\_LATEST). No initial value, no conflation.

### Which to use
- StateFlow for UI state (a loading flag, a list, the current user) where a new collector must see the current snapshot. It is what replaced LiveData in modern Android.
- SharedFlow with `replay = 0` for one-shot events such as a snackbar or a navigation command. Be ready for the follow-up: a dropped event is invisible, which is why many teams model events as part of the state and have the UI acknowledge them instead.

Collect them lifecycle-aware or you keep work running behind a backgrounded screen: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` in Compose, and `repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { flow.collect { } }` inside `lifecycleScope.launch` in a Fragment or Activity. Turn a cold repository flow into state with `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)`, which keeps the upstream alive across a rotation but stops it once the screen is really gone.

Cancellation and exception handling are two separate mechanisms, and `CancellationException` is the one you must never swallow.

### Cancellation
- **It is cooperative** — a coroutine only notices at a suspension point or when it checks `isActive`. A tight CPU loop with no suspension never cancels.
- `CancellationException` is normal control flow, not a failure, so it has to propagate. Raise it inside long computations with `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()`.
- `withContext(NonCancellable) { ... }` inside a `finally` is the sanctioned way to run cleanup that must complete after cancellation.
- A broad `catch (e: Exception)` around suspending code silently eats cancellation. Rethrow CancellationException first, or catch narrower types. `runCatching` has exactly the same trap.

### Exceptions
- With a regular Job the first child failure cancels the parent and every sibling.
- `SupervisorJob` and `supervisorScope` keep a failure isolated to the child that failed.
- `CoroutineExceptionHandler` catches what `launch` throws, and only in the root coroutine of a scope; it is ignored for `async`.
- `async` stores the failure in its Deferred and rethrows it from `await()` — but an `async` whose result is never awaited still cancels its parent scope.

A search box needs `debounce` to wait for a pause in typing, `distinctUntilChanged` to drop repeats, and `flatMapLatest` to cancel the request the next keystroke made obsolete.

### The pipeline, in order
1. The query starts as a `MutableStateFlow<String>` the UI writes on every change.
2. `debounce(300)` waits for the typing to stop before letting a value through.
3. `filter { it.length >= 2 }` skips queries too short to be worth a round trip.
4. `distinctUntilChanged()` drops a value equal to the previous one, which is what saves you when the user deletes a character and types it again.
5. `flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }` switches to the new inner flow and CANCELS the previous one, so an in-flight request for an old query is dropped instead of racing the new one.
6. `catch { emit(SearchState.Error) }` keeps an upstream failure from killing the collector, and `retryWhen` handles transient network errors.
7. `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Empty)` turns it into screen state.

### The distinctions an interviewer follows up with
- `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous inner flow, `flatMapConcat` queues them in order, `flatMapMerge` runs them concurrently and interleaves the results.
- `combine` re-emits whenever EITHER source changes, using the latest of the other — the right tool for query plus filters. `zip` pairs emissions one to one and waits for both sides, so a fast source is throttled by the slow one.
- `mapLatest` is the same cancel-the-previous behaviour for a plain transform rather than a nested flow.

By default a flow is sequential — `emit` suspends until the collector has finished with the previous value, so the producer runs at the collector's pace and nothing is ever dropped.

That default is often what you want, and when it is not, four operators change it:
- `buffer(capacity)` — runs the producer and the collector in separate coroutines with a channel between them, so their times overlap instead of adding up. `onBufferOverflow` picks SUSPEND, DROP\_OLDEST or DROP\_LATEST.
- `conflate()` — a buffer of one that keeps only the newest value. The collector always processes the latest state and silently skips what it missed, which is right for progress and sensor readings and wrong for events.
- `collectLatest { }` — does not drop the value, it cancels the collector BODY when a newer value arrives, then restarts it. Ideal when the body is a cancellable render or a suspending write.
- `mapLatest` / `transformLatest` — the same cancel-and-restart for an intermediate operator.

The other half of this question is context. `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` changes the dispatcher of everything UPSTREAM of it and leaves the collector where it was, and it introduces a buffer as a side effect. What you must never do is call `withContext` inside a `flow { }` builder: emissions have to happen in the collector's context, and the runtime throws IllegalStateException about a violated flow invariant. If you genuinely need to emit from several coroutines at once, `channelFlow` allows it because it hands you a thread-safe `send`.

A `suspend` function compiles to a state machine that takes an extra `Continuation` parameter and returns a marker value when it needs to pause.

### What the transform does
- The signature `suspend fun load(id: Long): User` becomes, on the JVM, `load(long, Continuation<User>): Any?` — it returns either the finished value or the internal COROUTINE\_SUSPENDED marker.
- The body is chopped at every suspension point into the branches of a switch over a label field, and the local variables that must survive a pause become fields of a generated Continuation object.
- Resuming means calling `continuation.resumeWith(result)`, which re-enters the same function at the stored label. The dispatcher is a ContinuationInterceptor that decides which thread that resumption happens on.

The consequences are the interesting part: a paused coroutine is one small object rather than a parked thread stack, which is why hundreds of thousands of them fit in memory; `suspend` is invisible to Java, which sees the Continuation parameter; and a suspend function cannot be called from ordinary code without a builder such as `launch`, `async` or `runBlocking`.

To bridge a callback API you build that Continuation yourself with `suspendCancellableCoroutine`: resume it exactly once from the callback, and register `invokeOnCancellation` to unsubscribe or cancel the underlying request when the coroutine is cancelled. Resuming twice throws. For an API that delivers many values instead of one, the equivalent is `callbackFlow` with `awaitClose` doing the unregistration.

The kotlinx-coroutines-test library swaps in a scheduler with a virtual clock, so delays complete instantly and in a deterministic order.

### The pieces
- `runTest { }` gives you a TestScope whose `delay(10_000)` returns immediately, and it fails the test if a child coroutine is still running at the end.
- `StandardTestDispatcher` queues new coroutines rather than running them: nothing progresses until `runCurrent()`, `advanceTimeBy(ms)` or `advanceUntilIdle()`. That is what lets you assert on the Loading state before the result arrives.
- `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` starts each coroutine eagerly instead, which is simpler when you only care about the final state.
- `Dispatchers.setMain(dispatcher)` in a `@Before` and `Dispatchers.resetMain()` in an `@After`, because `viewModelScope` runs on the main dispatcher, which does not exist on the JVM.
- Inject dispatchers rather than hardcoding them, so background work lands on the same test scheduler and stays controllable.

Collecting a StateFlow in a test is the part people get wrong: it never completes, so `toList()` hangs forever. Either collect into `backgroundScope`, which `runTest` cancels for you, or use Turbine — `vm.state.test { assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem()) }` — which also fails loudly on an unexpected extra emission. Remember that StateFlow conflates, so an intermediate state your test never observes may simply have been skipped rather than never set.

Coroutines give you no thread safety for free, because the default dispatcher runs them in parallel across as many threads as the device has cores.

### Fixes, cheapest first
- Do not share. Have each coroutine RETURN its result and combine at the end, or funnel every change through one `MutableStateFlow` and mutate it with `update { it + 1 }`, which is an atomic compare-and-set loop. Writing `state.value = state.value + 1` is a read-modify-write and loses updates exactly like the naive counter.
- An atomic for a single primitive: `AtomicInteger` on the JVM, or the `atomicfu` library in shared Kotlin code.
- `Mutex().withLock { }` when several fields must change together. It suspends instead of blocking, so it costs no thread. It is NOT reentrant — taking the same lock inside a block that already holds it deadlocks.
- `Semaphore(n)` when you want at most n coroutines inside a section, such as limiting concurrent uploads.
- **Confinement**: run every mutation through one thread with `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1)`, which replaces the old habit of allocating a single-thread executor that you then have to close.

What not to do: `synchronized` or a `ReentrantLock` around suspending code. You cannot suspend while holding a JVM monitor without pinning the thread, and blocking a dispatcher thread starves every other coroutine sharing the pool. `@Volatile` is also not a fix — it publishes a value to other threads but makes nothing atomic.

If the code only ever touches the counter from the main dispatcher, there is no race at all. That confinement is worth stating out loud, because it is why plenty of UI state needs no synchronization.

`async` starts each call immediately and `awaitAll` waits for the whole set, while `coroutineScope` guarantees that a failure cancels the siblings before it propagates.

- Inside `coroutineScope { }`, start each call with `async { }` and await afterwards. The calls overlap because `async` starts eagerly by default; total time becomes the slowest call rather than the sum.
- `awaitAll(a, b, c)` fails fast: the first exception cancels the other children and is rethrown from the scope, so you never leak a request whose result nobody will use.
- Partial results are a different requirement. Use `supervisorScope` so one child's failure does not cancel its siblings, and wrap each await so the screen can render what did arrive.
- `withTimeout(2_000) { }` throws TimeoutCancellationException and cancels the work inside; `withTimeoutOrNull` gives you null instead, which is usually nicer for an optional section of a screen.

The mistake this question exists to catch is accidental sequencing. `val a = async { first() }.await()` followed by `val b = async { second() }.await()` is fully sequential, and so is a plain `first(); second()` in one coroutine — the `async` only helps when both are started before the first `await`. If a call is genuinely optional, `async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY)` defers it until someone awaits.

One more thing worth saying: a suspending client such as Retrofit, Room or Ktor already moves off the calling thread, so wrapping these calls in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` adds nothing.
